Where Rephidim lay is not settled, and Ellicott is candid that the route is uncertain. He sets out three ways of reaching the valley where most critics place it, rejects the shortest because it passes an Egyptian settlement they would have avoided, and prefers the circuitous one as very open and so suitable for a vast host; he observes that the name means resting-places, which suits the most fertile spot in the peninsula, though the brook there has been known to fail. Keil spends his space refusing identifications rather than proposing one, ruling out a site too far from Sinai to be reached in a day and a spring whose valley is too narrow for a nation and whose well, never dry, answers neither to the want of water nor to the rock in Horeb. Henry begins where the difficulty really begins, that they journeyed at the commandment of the Lord, led by the pillar, and yet came where there was no water; from which he takes it that a man may be in the way of his duty and still meet troubles brought for the trial of his faith. Wesley repeats that sentence almost word for word.

On the chiding they divide between excusing and condemning. Ellicott comes nearest to excusing: water was scarce on that road, what they carried from Elim would be spent, and the needs of their children and cattle sharpened the thirst, so nothing but a lively faith could have kept a people patient in such an extremity. He will not soften what they said, for it was not faith that spoke but wrath; and their fear was no exaggeration, since thirst kills more surely and quickly than hunger, whole armies having died of it and crews perished at sea with water on every side and none to drink. Calvin condemns without qualification. Scarcely was the sedition about food quieted before they rebelled about drink; had they wanted bread and water at once they would have been more excusable, but to murmur after being fed from heaven was intolerable perversity, the double charge of chiding and tempting both growing from unbelief whose root was ingratitude. He adds the test they failed: they knew fountains cannot be made by mortal men, so why quarrel with Moses instead of calling on God, when a spark of faith would have sent them to prayer. Clarke makes the same point briefly, that God was their leader and all murmuring against Moses was reckoned against him.

The order to go out before the people strikes Calvin as hard, since it exposed Moses to immediate danger, and he observes that Moses neither trembled nor retreated; the taking of the elders only he reads as a middle course, keeping the glory of the miracle from being obscured while showing the multitude unworthy to witness it. Wesley draws the mercy out of the same order: the rod was carried not to summon a plague but to fetch water, and God maintains those at war with him, giving not a spring merely, as he showed one to Hagar, but water out of a rock. Gill notes that the Lord stood there not as a spectator but to direct where the blow should fall. Clarke takes the rock to be one Moses already knew from keeping Jethro's flocks, and reports the argument from its remains, that the supply must have been vast to serve so great a host, which excludes artifice, and that holes and channels are still shown in the stone. Ellicott agrees the rock must be one known beforehand and rules out the traditional site as too far from Rephidim. On the two names, Ellicott gives their roots, trial and quarrel. Clarke and Calvin both take the rock for a type of Christ on the apostle's authority, and both add the same warning, that many who drank perished notwithstanding.
8:
Amalek enters as a nation here, and the expositors differ on what brought them. Gill breaks from the rest by denying the Esau descent, making them descendants of Cush who were in being long before Amalek the grandson of Esau; Ellicott, Keil, Clarke, Henry and Wesley all take the ordinary line that they sprang from Esau's grandson. From there the readings diverge. Henry and Wesley — Wesley again condensing Henry almost word for word — treat the attack as hereditary malice, the old grudge over the birthright and blessing running in the blood, aggravated now that the promise was moving toward its accomplishment. Clarke declines that motive, comparing the Amalekites to the wandering Arabs who plunder caravans in the same desert: the baggage was the object, and the women, children and infirm at the rear were killed because they were found with it. Ellicott alone allows them a grievance, reading the Sinai region as their own summer and autumn pasture, occupied in their absence by emigrants who threatened to seize the rest; their hostility, he says, was not altogether unprovoked. Keil supplies the same seasonal logic, likening their presence near Sinai to the Bedouin who still leave the lower districts at the beginning of summer for cooler mountain grazing. Calvin holds two causes at once: their jealousy over the lost birthright, and God's own purpose to humble a people grown wanton in tranquillity.

Joshua is named here for the first time, and the commentators fill the silence from what follows. Ellicott makes him an Ephraimite of about forty-five, still called Hoshea and probably known already for military capacity; Clarke notes that the Septuagint and the Greek Testament alike render the name Jesus, and treats him as a type too evident to need pointing out: he conquered his people's enemies, brought them into the land and divided it by lot. Gill has him a man of war from his youth. On why Moses did not fight, Ellicott is plain that he judged himself unfit and passed the command on, adding one suggestion: a select body rather than the unwieldy mass; Calvin suspects a reason on God's side, that Moses was withdrawn from the leadership to humble the people's pride. What all agree on is the division of labour, and here Wesley reproduces Henry almost exactly: God qualifies his people for, and calls them to, various services for the good of his church — Joshua fights, Moses prays, and both minister to Israel.

The raised hand is where the readings part most sharply. Henry takes the rod held up as banner and appeal at once, animating soldiers who could see the rod that had summoned the plagues, and pleading with God that the battle was his. Ellicott doubts the Israelites could discern the movements, and puts the lesson elsewhere: God made the fortunes of the fight vary with Moses' hand to teach the value of intercessory prayer; Moses, Aaron and Hur were struck by the coincidence. Clarke refuses a literal mechanism, since lifting or lowering the hands could not humanly influence a battle, and reads the gesture as prayer with a double reference — help comes from God alone, and supplication is necessary to prevail. Gill records Aben Ezra's objection to the banner reading, that Aaron or Hur would then have fixed the rod where it could be seen, and cites the Targums for the prayer gesture, as Clarke does. On the failing hands Henry and Gill both draw the lesson against themselves, that the more spiritual the service the more apt we are to flag: Joshua's hands were not heavy in fighting, but Moses' were. Calvin knows the allegories that make Aaron and Hur the two Testaments and the stone Christ, and sets them aside as having more acuteness than solidity: Moses mistrusted his own weakness, and therefore sought two assistants.
14:
The command to write brings out the sharpest divergence over what writing meant this early. Clarke calls it the first mention of writing on record and admits he cannot tell what it signified; he suspects the verse anticipates a later command, and thinks the first regular alphabetical writing was that on the two tables of stone, which came later, so the memorial here may have been some symbolic registration. Wesley makes the same observation, that this is the first mention of writing in scripture and the command was perhaps not given until after the law was written on stone. Ellicott moves the other way entirely: the Hebrew reads in the book, and he takes that definite article, supported by Egyptian papyri long anterior to Moses, as implying a book already in existence in which God's dealings were entered from time to time, probably the germ of the Pentateuch. Calvin dismisses the whole dispute about the book as superfluous, since God simply wills that the memory should never perish. On the rehearsing in Joshua's ears the two agree: Clarke that it marked Joshua out as successor, Calvin that it was to keep him from fainting under the difficulties awaiting.

The altar divides them over whether anything was offered on it. Gill places it on Horeb or the hilltop and says thank-offerings were sacrificed there, or at least a monument raised; Ellicott makes sacrifice the primary purpose and the memorial secondary, noting that altars are otherwise unnamed apart from Jacob's El-Elohe-Israel, and that a name would help keep the event in remembrance. Keil observes flatly that nothing is said about sacrifices at all, and infers that the altar and its expressive name served as memorial and watchword rather than a place of offering. On the name itself Clarke presses the military figure hardest: the hands and rod of Moses were held up as soldiers hold their standards, and since standards bear the arms of the country, the name of Jehovah became the armorial bearing of the whole congregation, each man not his own but the Lord's soldier. Ellicott expressly rejects that link — it is not clear, he says, that the rod is the banner in any sense; the banner is Jehovah himself. Calvin refuses the rendering miracle, holding the word always means banner, and finds the altar's object in keeping Israel from boasting of their own strength. Wesley, again close to Henry, ends where the altar does: he that does all the work should have all the praise.

The closing verse is where the sources admit they are working in the dark, and one of them denies it. Keil calls the expression obscure, chiefly because of the unique word rendered throne, and rehearses the old versions; Ellicott answers that the Hebrew can scarcely be called obscure, since it plainly gives the marginal sense, that Amalek lifted his hand against God's throne and therefore God will war against him. Gill sets out both options, the oath reading followed by the Targum of Jonathan, Jarchi and Aben Ezra, and Drusius's objection that God should not swear by what Christ prohibited; Gill takes the hand to be Amalek's. Calvin sets aside both the oath and the reading that makes the throne the Church, and takes the hand upon the throne to mean that God does not sit idly in heaven as the Epicureans imagine, but exercises dominion. Clarke goes furthest from the received text, reporting Houbigant's conjecture that throne is a copyist's error for ensign, the two Hebrew letters being easily confused, and Bate's suggestion that a hand holding a cup of wrath was carved on an altar stone; Clarke prefers Houbigant. On the fulfilment they converge: Clarke dates it to Saul four hundred and twelve years later, Calvin notes the long delay, and Ellicott traces it through Saul and David to its completion under Hezekiah.
